utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Tuesday, April 7th, 2009. I would like to greet the accused, notably Mr. Coric, who is back with us. I also would like to greet counsels for Defence, all members of the OTP, and everyone helping us. I will first give the floor to our Registrar, because I believe he has an IC number to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 2D has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to its documents tendered through Witness Dragutin Cehulic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC986. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Trial Chamber is going to now issue two oral decisions, the first one on the visit of the family of Mr. Praljak when he will be testifying in this case. At the hearing of the 1st of April, 2009, the accused Praljak asked the Chamber to let his family members visit him for the time he will be testifying as a witness as part of his defence. The Trial Chamber notes that it is only the Registry who can organise these visits at the UNDU. The Trial Chamber also notes that the accused Praljak is due to testify for two months, approximately. The Trial Chamber feels that there are no grounds that warrant a prohibition of these visits, due to the fact that his testimony will last a very long time. Second oral decision, decision on the motion made by the Stojic Defence to add Exhibit 2D01533 on its 65 ter(G) list. On April 4th, 2009, the Stojic Defence filed a motion to add Exhibit 2D01533, which is an order by Bruno Stojic, dated March 22nd, 1993, and addressing the appointment of lower-ranking officers within the Herceg Stjepan Brigade on its 65 ter(G) list in order to show it to Witness Drago Juric. During the hearing of April 6th, 2009, the Stojic Defence told the Trial Chamber that it had postponed the testimony of Witness Drago Juric from April 6 and 7, 2009, to April 27 and 28, 2009. The Trial Chamber notes that Exhibit 2D01533 addresses the power held by the accused Bruno Stojic in relation to appointments and is interesting in light of the interpretation of Article 34 of the Decree on Armed Forces of the HZ-HB. The Trial Chamber believes that the Stojic Defence did not demonstrate that Exhibit 2D01533 is essential to the case of the accused Stojic, as required on paragraph 26 of the 8th guide-line defined in the Trial Chamber's decision of April 24th, 2008. The Trial Chamber notes that it has already heard enough evidence on this item. Therefore, on these grounds and given that the motion was filed extremely late, the Trial Chamber decides to dismiss Bruno Stojic's motion to add an exhibit. So in a nutshell, the Trial Chamber believed that this exhibit was not necessary, given the abundance of evidence that we already have on this, and it was not necessary to add it to the 65 ter list. Mr. Kovacic, if you are very brief, please start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be brief. The Prosecutor, on the 3rd of April, made a submission, Prosecution response to Praljak's notice regarding the upcoming statements, pursuant to Rules 84 and 84 bis. Your Honours, in procedural terms, this is an erroneous title, because the title of the submission is "Response," although it is a request for the Trial Chamber to hand down some decisions. A response cannot call for any decisions to be made, and for procedural reasons this submission should be rejected. We cannot respond to their submissions, since the Prosecution decided to call it a response. Very simply, we don't see any basis for you to allow us to reply to that. And actually it is a reply to our notice, and the notice does not require a response. The Prosecution could have filed a notice or a motion. This situation is not clear, and we deem that, in procedural terms, this is a mistake. And the second issue is this: The Prosecution do not demonstrate any dignity towards this Tribunal, because the Trial Chamber has already handed down a decision on the right of General Praljak to be able to continue his testimony according to Rule 84 and 84 bis. Thus, the decision has been made, and in that sense the Prosecution could have reacted at the moment when the decision was handed down, and that was a long time ago, many months ago. There was no reason for them to stall their response for such a long time. And the third argument that I would like you to bear in mind is this: We planned for General Praljak's defence based on the previous decision made by the Trial Chamber, which said that they would allow for an additional statement or testimony, and we prepared everything based on that presumption, based on that decision, and now the Prosecution responds and debates whether this was correct or not. There are some other elements there, but I don't want to go into details, because I just want it to be noted that we object to this submission, for formal and legal reasons, and that we do not want to reply in writing, because we simply don't know how to react, because this submission was made contrary to any Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your position is noted on the transcript. The Coric Defence and then Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just briefly. Mr. Coric's Defence would like to propose an ex parte session after today's session, and the subject will be health issues and the health condition of Mr. Coric. We are kindly requesting to the Trial Chamber to make the decision as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will try to be brief. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Mr. President, each of Your Honours, Counsel, all those in and around the courtroom. Ever so briefly, Mr. President: I'm disappointed and find it unfortunate that for the last some days now, Mr. Kovacic seems absolutely determined to accuse the Prosecution of bad faith on every possible occasion. This is form over substance. The Praljak Defence filed a pleading that they called "Notice." I can't -- the Prosecution can't control, of course, what they put on the face of their pleading -- called it a notice, taking a position, and I think it's entirely appropriate for the Prosecution in such a situation to file a response to information provided to the Chamber, asking -- either stating or asserting that certain action will take place. So I think it was entirely appropriate for us to make our views known. If the problem is that Mr. Kovacic is concerned whether he can make a response or not, then of course it's up to the Chamber to grant him whatever leave the Chamber deems appropriate, but it would be simply form over substance to say that the Prosecution could somehow be held silent and simply not to respond or make its position known in response to a pleading filed by the Defence. Now in connection, Your Honour, one -- 30 seconds more: In connection with Mr. Kovacic's repeated assertions that the issue has already been resolved, I think with the greatest respect, Your Honour, and I do mean this with the utmost respect, I think the earlier commentary in the transcript was that the Mr. President was preliminarily of the view that it would be allowed. I do not believe there is a Trial Chamber decision on the topic of whether Mr. Praljak will, in fact, be allowed to make a second opening statement, and we have stated our position on that, Your Honours. And even if I'm wrong in my understanding of the transcript, that would nonetheless be our position. And given the history in this case to date, which includes, I might remind the Chamber, the denial of Mr. Prlic's attempt to make a second statement, inconsistent with that ruling and inconsistent -- I think the better practice in these proceedings to date, the Prosecution indeed does oppose any second opening statement by the Praljak -- by Mr. Praljak or his Defence. He has done that. The Rules provides for one opening statement. He did so. It's time to move on. If he wants to be heard again, he can take the witness stand, take the oath, and give his testimony like all other witnesses. And that's the position, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning [as interpreted], sir -- good afternoon. Could you please give me your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Davor Korac. 10 September 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation at the moment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a degree in Economics, and I am working for a private company, dealing in the trade of goods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in a court regarding what happened in the former Yugoslavia or this is the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down. Let me give you some information on what will happen. You are going to answer questions put to you by Ms. Nozica. She might show you a number of documents; I don't know yet. Then after this stage, maybe the other counsel of Defence will also put questions to you, and then the Prosecution -- the Prosecutor will cross-examine you, if need be. And the Judges on the Bench can also put questions to you if they believe that it is useful. Please try and be brief in your answers. And if you don't understand the meaning of a question, just ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Before I begin, I would like to say that my examination may last longer than an hour. I hope not, but given the Prosecutor's objections that we have received recently, and our replies, with regard to the documents in respect of Mr. Dragutin Cehulic, I believe that the Trial Chamber has seen that for this witness we have three documents that consist of several invoices. The witness has seen all these documents, but at this moment, in order to avoid any risk of future objections and possible decisions on the part of the Trial Chamber which might disallow the admission of these documents, I am prepared to go over all of these documents with the witness, and that's why my examination-in-chief might take longer than originally foreseen, which was an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica, to save time, you can say that you went through a number of documents with the witness, this document, that document. He'll say, "Yes, I saw it," and so forth and so on. There is no need to introduce a huge number of documents just to say one thing, which is why we issued the oral decision earlier, so you would understand that it's pointless to add tonnes of documents that are all of the same meaning. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I will act according to your instruction. But when we come to the topic, we will see why it may be significant to establish the total number of the invoices in question. I will come to that when we come to the documents, and then we will see whether it is necessary to show a large number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Korac.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll start my examination-in-chief in the following way: I'm going to present your particulars, and then at the end you will just tell me whether the particulars are correct or not. You graduated from the School of Economics in 1984 in Sarajevo. On the 1st of July, 1991, until 27 June 1992, you worked in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. You were the chief of the -- of a department in the Administration for Financial Affairs. Together with your family, you left Sarajevo on the 27th of June, 1992, and you moved to Neum. From September 1992 to September 1994, you were a member of the HVO Battalion in Neum. You returned to Sarajevo in May 1996, and you have lived and worked in Sarajevo ever since. Currently, you are an employee of a private company which trades in automobiles. Is all this correct, Mr. Korac?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, from the 1st of July, 1991, to the 27th of June, 1992, you were the chief of a finance department in the Administration for Finances of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Korac, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the assistant head of that same administration, Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Which other departments made part of that administration?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: In addition to my department for finances, there was also a department for property, legal and residential affairs, as well as another department for finances.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was the job; i.e., what did you do in the department that you headed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I had several desk officers, several warehouse officers, several accountants who were keeping books, and we also engaged in the procurement and distribution of materiel and technical equipment at the level of the Ministry of the Interior for the territory of the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did your department carry out the annual stock-taking of all the equipment of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, there was stock-taking every year on the 31st of December, and that was one of the main tasks of the administration and the department at the level of the ministry for the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, how long did Mr. Bruno Stojic keep coming to work and keep performing his duties as the assistant minister of the Ministry of the Interior in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I was aware that Mr. Bruno Stojic's family resided in Neum. We all knew that, and we knew that almost every weekend he went to see his family there and that he returned to work on Mondays. And as far as I know, on the first Monday in April 1992, Mr. Bruno Stojic did not come back to work. And that weekend, Sarajevo had been blocked for very well-known reasons, and after that weekend nobody could come back into Sarajevo or leave Sarajevo through regular routes. As far as I know, it was then that Mr. Stojic stopped coming back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you or anybody else in the service have telephone contacts with Mr. Stojic after that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes. For a certain while after the events in question, Mr. Bruno Stojic's secretary told us on several occasions that the boss, as she called him, meaning Mr. Stojic, kept calling, explaining why he could not come to work, although we all knew what the reason was. And I believe that on two occasions, he wanted to talk to me as well, and I did talk to him. And I believe that this went on until the moment the post office burnt down in Sarajevo, which meant that communication was interrupted. That was in May, in the first days of May of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, did you have frequent contacts with Mr. Bruno Stojic as part of your work?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I can say that that happened on a daily basis, as a result of my work commitments as the chief of department, but this was also true of other chiefs of departments that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, how will you describe to the Trial Chamber the attitude of Mr. Stojic towards his position as the assistant minister of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? How did he take his job?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Precisely so. While he was affiliated with the ministry, he behaved as an assistant minister of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is -- that was my impression, and that is my conviction as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain to the honourable Trial Chamber what you mean when you say that he behaved as the minister of the interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Looking in hindsight, if you had asked me that at the time, my answer may have been different, because it would not have been coloured by the events that took place subsequently. At the moment when it became important, what your name was, where you hailed from, what political options were closer to you and which ones were not so close to you, I can say that in the administration, which had several dozens of employees of various ethnic backgrounds, and if we apply all the other criteria that I use to divide people today that were first used at that time, Mr. Stojic did not have any problem with that, the employees did not have any problem with that. In addition to that, the Ministry of the Interior employed people from public security stations, from security services centres. There were 109 public security stations in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was never any problems with their ethnic background. A majority of people that I communicated with had a very positive view of the administration and its leadership. In that sense, I would say that there were no differences based on where people came from, from which organisational unit, in our job.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Chamber specifically if Mr. Bruno Stojic did his job and met all his obligations in the best interests of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, within the MUP itself, the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which body was it that took decisions?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: The ministry was headed by the minister, and the body that he works closely with was the minister's collegium, made up of the minister, his deputy, and the assistants of all the basic organisational units, the administrations within the ministry. Those were the people that he worked closely with, and you could call it the minister's collegium.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We've heard this quite many times in this courtroom, but maybe it would not be amiss to repeat once more. Who was the actual minister at the time, the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: At the time, it was Mr. Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Alija Delimustafic, Delimustafic; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, Delimustafic. Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's fine now. Can you tell us the names of other assistants? You said that the minister and the assistants made up the ministry's collegium. Can you tell us the names of some of the assistants, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me, there was the Communications Administration, the assistant was Mr. Akif Sabic; then there was the Crime Administration, headed by Mr. Momcilo Mandic; the Police Administration headed by Mr. Avdo Hebib, I believe; the Personnel Administration headed by Selimovic, Hilmo Selimovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is quite sufficient for our purposes. Can you now tell the Chamber about the relationship between Mr. Bruno Stojic and the members of the collegium? What were their relations like?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I think they worked quite well together. As far as their professional commitments were concerned, there were no delays or anything like that. Sometimes discussions were quite lively, which is on occasion necessary to get a job done properly, but there weren't any clashes between the members that one could observe. I believe I can say that their cooperation was obviously fair. Perhaps I should add this: This was a period at which certain things began happening, and many people later regretted that those things had ever happened. Nevertheless, at the time some of the members of this collegium worked together on a private basis and even socialised outside their work. They socialised quite frequently, as a matter of fact. I think the media followed this as well, the Sarajevo-based newspaper "Us" wrote about this on a weekly basis. Mr. Stojic, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Delimustafic would meet and socialise. One week, one of them hosted this little get-together, and the next week it would be someone else. They socialised. They would meet in public places, which in some way demonstrated that what we were watching on the TV news every night was not necessarily all true. It was a good thing to read about this in the papers every now and then, knowing that you were working in an environment in which people were socialising even on their own free time and of their own free will, and not just because they had to because of their work. The message that this was sending to everyone was that it was all right to live with people who were in many ways different. They were on very good terms. I'm not sure if they were friends, but they were certainly companions, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say or suggest that some sort of message was sent across by this, by them socialising. We've talked about this in the courtroom. We talked about all these divisions along party lines, along ethnic lines. Is this a message that got through? Did the public understand and take a positive lesson from this, that all these ministers and assistant ministers were socialising also on their own free time and that they weren't just linked to each other professionally but also socialised on a friendly basis, if you like?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, I think you could put it that way. For example, I had a colleague who I was working with. He was different in one way or another and I was different from him, but still we spent time together, we socialised. Had our superiors been sending out a different kind of signal, maybe that would have made it impossible for us, at a lower level, to socialise and hang out together.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now I'm going back to your professional work, to your line of duty. How was MTS procured in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: That was one of the commitments of the administration headed by Mr. Bruno Stojic. The work of my department was part of this overall effort. Obviously, initially there would be an order to obtain certain types of MTS, and this order would be issued by the assistant minister, Mr. Stojic. There would be requests and orders previously from the minister's collegium. Those orders and requests were in keeping with a document. I'm not sure if I'm interpreting this correctly. Nevertheless, procurement was always based on a programme of purchasing equipment and modernising the equipment of the MUP throughout the Republic of B and H. There would be a report that was drawn up invariably, containing a summary or an overview of the needs of public security stations across the country or security services centres, as well as the MUP itself, the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP being a very demanding service not just in terms of numbers but also in terms of actual equipment. A document like this would normally be produced on a mid-term basis and would span a four-year period routinely. Goods and equipment were then obtained based on this. There would be a budget that was allotted to this sort of activity, and this was down to the finance people. That was no longer my job. But I was there, I was working there, and I knew something about what was going on also at a government level, and then there would be a budget that was approved. It had to be ratified by the Parliament, as far as I know. And then based on this budget, there would be procurement, renewal, modernisation, and this applied to the Ministry of the Interior in its entirety. All sections would benefit from this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've told us a little about the modernisation programme right now. I think that was the phrase you used.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: "Equipment and modernisation." I think that's what the programme was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And the programme applied to which period? Tell us, please, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: The programme that applied at the time spanned the period between 1990 and 1995, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, could you please take the smaller binder in front of you. I would like to go through a number of documents covering some of the subjects that we have been discussing. The smallest binder that you have in front of you. The first document is 2D00836. Mr. Korac, what we see there is a letter dated the 16th of July, 1991, signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic, addressed to the Cabinet of the MUP and members of the collegium or the advisory board, a report on the possibility of a more rational use of the building of the Police Social Centre. That is how the heading reads. Can you, first of all, please, tell us where was this police hall?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: It was and it still is right in the center of town, in the immediate vicinity of the Ministry of the Interior building. The ministry was at Borisa Kovacevic Street, I'm not sure what the street's name is today. Perhaps 100 metres, as the crow flies; no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, and I believe you've read this letter in its entirety while being proofed, was this the usual procedure for an assistant minister of the interior to communicate with the minister's cabinet and members of the advisory board?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I think at a stage like this, and given the nature of the activity in question, this was a perfectly normal procedure for announcing an initiative. What I see here is perfectly clear. There had been a considerable investment, and the building had been revamped, if you like, several years before. It was used by the ministry. There were a lot of things going on there. There was a cinema hall. It had a hall for festivities of all kinds. It had a gym, all sorts of things, and it was hardly ever used. Sometimes there would be a ceremony that was held there, an occasion marked, or perhaps consultations took place there. Mr. Stojic is a natural talent. He was an economist and he was proposing here that instead of all this expenditure, instead of spending all this money, some money might be saved or poured back into the state coffers, and then those funds could be used to modernise the entire operation, the equipment and the building and everything. Obviously, the money in question is not a lot, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 2D88 -- 2D00814, please, that's the next -- 841, that's the next document. This is a proposal for analysis, sent by Bruno Stojic, assistant minister of the interior, on the 10th of December, 1991, addressed to the Republican Institute for Public Planning. There is an attachment here for drafting an analysis, the development of All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection, 1991, with an assessment of the possibility of development throughout 1992. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber why there was a need to draw up an analysis such as this one? Was the MUP under any obligation to provide an attachment like this, as done by Mr. Bruno Stojic in the case before us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: This wasn't exactly my line of work, not just when I worked in the MUP, but even before that time, I wasn't in charge of anything like this, but I do know that any economic entity, any social entity, any state entity, any federal entity, definitely had to deal with these issues, what we called at the time "All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection." They were also under an obligation to deal with issues that had to do with what was termed "Defence Preparations." The Ministry of the Interior was one of the two most significant players in these defence preparations, in addition to, of course, the federal army. Therefore, the ministry had every obligation to make plans to monitor developments and to make proposals for analyses like that to be drafted. I say more general level, the objective being to possibly have to defend the country from any attacks, attacks from abroad, obviously. Everyone had to deal with these issues, defence issues, in one way or another, but if you had an economic entity, or perhaps in the state ministries there was special sections for All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection, therefore it was probably even a special obligation for the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not just to be ready to face eventualities such as this one, but also to work hard to improve its own capacities, in terms of personnel, in terms of equipment, to keep modernising all the time so that it might be ready to respond to a possible threat or attack from abroad, attack on the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please now go to page 2. This is a draft proposal for the analysis. Let me just point you to page 1, the second-to-last passage. There is mention there of the budget for 1991, and you said that within the programme for modernisation and equipment, this is something you've been talking about, and then the budget was approved in relation to each and every year; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about the last paragraph? There is a proposed programme for the modernisation of the services of the public and social security in relation to 1991 to 1995, and you said it was between 1990 and 1995. You made a mistake there; it's actually from 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It's a matter of parentheses, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The document goes on to say that the programme talked about various needs, the need for weapons, for equipment, and then there is a list of various necessities, equipment needed by the Ministry of the Interior to be able to continue its activities?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At the end of this paragraph, it says that the programme should be adopted by the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the ministry had already submitted for review this proposal, and that the proposal was being reviewed by the government. Is that the same procedure that you were telling us about, in terms of procurement, equipment and everything else, and this was used as a basis for all the procurement that occurred back in 1991 and 1992; is this how it was adopted?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior based their expenditure on a budget, and obviously there had to be plans on how this money was to be used. Needless to say, again, this wasn't exactly part of my work, it wasn't something that I was dealing with directly, but I know that even nowadays, whenever there's a government proposal, you have parliaments and assemblies adopting budgets. I expect the same procedure applied at the time. The BH Assembly would adopt a budget in relation to whichever year was coming next. For example, in 1991, what was drawn up was a budget proposal for the following year, and then it would be submitted to the finance ministry, to the government, and there would need to be a couple of things that were harmonised. Not everything was necessarily approved, but what you eventually obtained was a budget that was normally a result of some sort of a compromise between what was needed and what was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Another document about this, 2D00840, another document about the same subject. Mr. Korac, it is precisely for this reason that I've been showing you these documents, because you were telling us this is exactly the sort of thing that is being done nowadays. I just want to know if this was the same thing that was done at the time, back then, the period we're talking about, whether the same procedures were -- I've been cautioned to slow down. I'll repeat this. That is precisely the reason I've been asking you all these questions, because I want to make sure, based on your knowledge, whether at the time the same procedures were followed and the same regulations that applied in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's why I would now like you to move on to the following document. That's the one that you have in front of you. Again, this is another document signed Mr. Bruno Stojic, and the document is dated the 21st of December, 1991. And again he's addressing the finance ministry, asking for additional funds to be used for the ministry's work. In this letter, Mr. Stojic points out that funds were needed, additional funds. Now he talks about the various sectors, expenditure, common funds, special-purpose funds, the public security service, that sort of thing. And then if we go down to the last paragraph, he expresses a hope and desire that the proposal would be adopted, as had been the case hitherto. Mr. Korac, what about this document dispatched by Mr. Stojic; was this document, too, in keeping with all the procedures that applied at the time on procurement and general expenditures of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I believe that a request of this kind is normal and correct, especially bearing in mind that if the budget was spent, which did not happen in January or February, usually it happens towards the end of the year, and in this case it is in November of that year, and the ministry did not have any more funds left, so it had to turn to the state, and I believe that the most normal and customary way was for them to address the Ministry of Finances in order to see whether there could -- there were any funds to be had in any of the reserves, or maybe this should have been something else, like the -- reconsidering the budget, but it was late, November was late to reconsider the budget, so he turned to the Ministry of Finances and this was a legal way to request additional funds for regular business. And here we can see that we're talking about the material spending, funds for joint spending, funds for the special purposes of the public security service, funds for special purposes of the Internal Affairs Training Centre, which was part of the ministry. So we're talking about the whole Ministry of the Interior which required additional funds.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When both you and I receive signals from the courtroom, that means we both have to slow down in order for everything that the two of us say be properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that I will be asking the witness about three documents that contain invoices for the purchase of a Golf car, and I am referring to the testimony by Witness Josip Manolic on the 4th of July, 2006, and his statement provided on pages 4386 through 4389. The Prosecutor showed the witness document P134 on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, in the course of 1991-1992, were Golf vehicles purchased for the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes. The purchases were made in keeping with the programme of equipping and modernisation that was in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to the best of your recollection, during the period 1991 and 1992, while you worked at the MUP, how many Golf vehicles were purchased pursuant to this plan of programme and -- of equipping and modernisation, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I know that there were several batches of supplies up to the end of 1991, and then up to the end of June 1992, maybe up to 300 vehicles were purchased for the Ministry of the Interior, in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which were covered by the programme that we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You have just mentioned it in passing, but I would like to seek some clarification from you. Does the programme -- did the programme actually specify who the vehicles were purchased for?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The programme was a sum of all the needs of all the public security stations, and I believe that there were a total of 109 of them in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were also nine centres of public security, and there was also the ministry which comprised the school for the training of the ministry employees. When all the needs were summed up, ones that had been coordinated, because you have to know that a public security station may request ten photocopying machines and the assistant has the right to say, You only need two, and then they compromise on five, this plan of equipping and modernisation is also the basis for the distribution of all the purchased equipment, because the equipment is usually procured based on a document of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You have used photocopying machines as an example. Would that apply to Golf vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Of course. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, how were the vehicles procured? According to you, there was this programme of modernisation and equipping, which displayed the needs of all the segments within the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After the programme was drafted, how were Golf vehicles procured? How were procurements done, in general?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Depending on what is being purchased and the -- let me limit myself to this particular case. The existence of the programme and the elements in the programme called "Cars" doesn't mean that the administration will embark on the procurement. If a conclusion is reached by the collegium that the time has come for some materiel and equipment to be purchased, then professional services, and in this case this was the Department for Materials Ordered and Finances, and particularly the -- its Detachment for Materials Ordered, they started collecting offers. Although there were no legal requirements or conditions in place for this to be three bids, in principle we always had to have at least three procurement bids that had to be accompanied by an elabora [phoen] that contained all the financial aspects, and when those arrived they would be handed over to the assistant minister, who would then get together with other colleagues and the minister, they would discuss the bids and they would make their decision based on all the accompanying materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Should I understand that, that the final decision was in the hands of the collegium of ministers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who was the authorised person to sign payment orders for a procurement of this kind?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I believe it was only the minister who was allowed to sign such payment orders, or he could have authorised somebody else. But I believe that he was the only authorised person to execute such payment orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have three documents here that contain certain invoices relative to the purchase of Golf vehicles. Could you please look at document 2D00839. Could you please tell the honourable Trial Chamber whether the invoices that you can see in the document, whether they refer -- and I'm starting with invoice number 9100286 up to number 9100315. Do all these invoices refer to the purchase of the Golf vehicles that we have discussed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes. Since I have already had an occasion to look at the copies of the invoices, I can say that, yes, the invoices in question refer to the purchase of the vehicles for the Ministry of the Interior in the course of 1991 -- 1991. Here we can see clearly who was selected as the seller. This was Adria Auto, based in Dubrovnik. The buyer was the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You can see the date of the invoice. You can see the basic data of the car, the price, the chassis number. You can see all that. And in the heading of almost every document, you can see who the vehicle was intended for, and this was all in keeping with the programme for equipping and modernisation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You're looking at invoice number, and I'm going to give you the last three digits, 286; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you see what is written in handwriting because the interpreter could not discern clearly what is written here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I believe it is for Bihac, for the public security station in Bihac. Indeed, it is not easy to read, but since I was very familiar with the procedure and this particular purchase, I know where it was intended for.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at 287. That's the next invoice. Was that another Golf?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was another car of almost the same characteristics. The only things that differ were the chassis number and the engine number, and I believe that its destination was the Police Administration. That's what you can see in the heading of the invoice.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the following invoice. The number is 288.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the same vehicle. The date is 16th September. It says "Golf vehicle." It gives you the price and everything else. It says "Garage" here, and I believe that the reference is made to the garage that existed within the building of the Ministry of the Interior. And those vehicles were used by the ministry, for the official purposes of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please look at the following invoice, which is 289.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes. In the heading, you can't see a destination, but you can see something that looks like the DIN number of the registration plate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Of what town?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please look at invoice number 290.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes. The same or similar vehicle, same period, the month of September, so it would be the same batch. This is the fifth administration, i.e., administration within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, would you be so kind as to explain to the Chamber what the interest and relevance of the next document is, which looks to us like the previous one, and the next again like the previous one? What's the interest in having X number of identical documents? I would be really grateful if you could pick out one of those that have anything special to them. I think that would be quite enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I fully agree with my fellow Judge. We know that the Ministry of Interior bought Golf cars. We know that they were sent to different police stations, administrations and so on. All this is explained, so let's not waste any time talking about every invoice a lot and every car that is sent to each and every police station. Ask a question, you know, to shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I believe that it was clear, when I referred to the part of the transcript, i.e., part of the examination of Witness Josip Manolic. Josip Manolic quoted from documents that I mentioned, document 134, P134, part of the statement by Mr. Boban, who says that Mr. Bruno Stojic purchased through the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina a total of 150 Golf for the HZ-HB. I believe that it is very relevant to see that during that period of time a total of 260 Golfs were purchased, as one can see from the documents, and I also believe that it is very relevant to establish where the Golfs were dispatched to. I fully accept your suggestion. I did not intend to read all 260 invoices, because we have a witness here who looked at all of them, but I just wanted to present to the Trial Chamber how we can establish where the Golfs were sent to, and that's why I asked the witness to explain some of the invoices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Ms. Nozica. The simplest thing is to ask the question in the following manner: Tell him that a witness, Mr. Josip Malovic [as interpreted], said that 150 vehicles had been bought and sent to police stations. "You took part in this, Mr. Witness, so can you confirm it?" And then the witness can answer, "Yes, and as a matter of fact the invoices that we have just seen together prove this."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I would like to proceed to see whether 150 Golfs were, indeed, sent to where Mr. Boban said that they were, or maybe the situation was entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Nozica. But whether its 150, 200 or 300, that's pointless.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate that, and I will go through the documents very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, have you had an opportunity to look at all the invoices contained in 2D839?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you confirm to the Trial Chamber that these are indeed invoices that were issued on the 16th of March, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise. 16th of September. Can you also confirm that each of the invoices or at least -- or most of them mentions the destination of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the somewhat thicker binder which contains 2D837. Can you confirm for the sake of the Trial Chamber that these are invoices for the purchase of Golf vehicles that were also purchased within the framework of the same project that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, these are the documents that I previously went through, and they are about the same purchase. It's a different lot, that's all. These were invoiced on the 31st of December and then distributed based on a predetermined distribution plan, which was also a basis on which these vehicles were purchased. They were distributed to the Security Services Centres, and this is a note that's handwritten on most of these invoices.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, can you confirm, for the benefit of the Chamber, 9100346 through 9100578? I'm talking about these invoices. You have gone through these, each of these, and can you now confirm that that is the purchase that we're talking about when vehicles were purchased?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you further confirm that while looking at most of these documents, in the heading we see who the cars were eventually dispatched to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just another document on this same subject. That's in the smaller binder, 2D00838.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I hadn't intended to ask any question because it's a well-known topic, but there's one question regarding budget techniques, for those who know about finance. These invoices are dated December 31st. Was it because the budget that had been decided for 1991 be completely -- be finished in order to use up all the funds that had been allotted to these lines, to these; otherwise, there would have been a problem, probably, to transfer the purchases to the next year? In a word, aren't these invoices dated December 31st in order to just use all the spending that had been planned in the first place when the budget was drafted earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether that was the intention, but when dealing with budgets, if there are any funds that are unused, the funds do not just go back, they're not returned. Therefore, it is only logical that the funds would be used in the same year for which they are earmarked.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you to look at 2D00838, please. Witness, there is a total of ten invoices there. The date is the 10th of March, 1992. Can you please tell the Chamber about these ten Golf vehicles? Were they purchased as part of the equipping and modernisation plan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the third lot or batch, or one of the batches of these vehicles that were delivered in March 1992. We're talking about the same funds. We're talking about the same provider. This is part of the same deal. It is just that the invoices don't make it perfectly clear who they were sent to or allocated to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Finally, in order to see what the source is, 2D843. That is the source for all these documents. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a letter by the director of the Federal Ministry of the Interior and the Federal Police Administration, Mr. Zlatko Miletic, sending this to the office of attorney-at-law Senka Nozica. He specifies here that he had received a request from my office in order to forward these invoices to Senka Nozica, attorney-at-law, representing Mr. Stojic, which he did. Do you know Mr. Zlatko Miletic, and do you know for a fact that this was his position at the time, as specified here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I don't personally know him, but I know he held the position at the time. Mr. Miletic is a well-known person in those circles. I'm a well-informed citizen, like many others, and I know that this indeed was the position he held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, having gone through all these invoices, could you perhaps tell the Chamber whether these vehicles were distributed or delivered across Bosnia-Herzegovina to each and every public security station, to Security Services Centres across Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, the vehicles that I've looked at, the vehicles that we're talking about, were distributed in keeping with the procurement plan, which was also the distribution plan. It was for public security stations and security services centres or stations across Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, were you involved in the drafting of the regular annual list of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for 1991, the stock-taking?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes, that was part of the work of my administration, the administration headed by Mr. Bruno Stojic. We had to do an annual stock-taking, listing all of the items, equipment. And I'm not just talking about basic things, such as cars, but also weapons, stationery, money, requests, and so on and so forth. In one word, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me about these Golf vehicles in 1991. Was stock-taking of all these vehicles at the end of 1991, and were these vehicles included in the lists?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: All of the equipment, including motor vehicles and these Golf vehicles, all items and goods that were eventually distributed and delivered to public security stations, security services centres, by the 31st of December found their way into the lists and were later included in the report of the stock-taking commission, and that was the final document that was produced in relation to any big expenditures over the previous year.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were there any discrepancies once the job was done, in terms of was the documents reflected and what was really the case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: You're asking me about these vehicles; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: No, none. Even as far as the basic equipment were concerned, and then cars were part of this, there were no discrepancies between what the books reflected and the real situation. But every time an inventory was drawn up, every time there was some stock-taking, damaged or out-of-date items would be listed, and I assume some items were set apart, but not a great quantity. For example, there was supposed to be something that was at the Jajce Public Security Station, and yet this something was stolen. There was nothing like that that occurred in any of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have some information indicating that some irregularities occurred in the way that cars were distributed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: This certainly wasn't something that I encountered in my work. It wasn't my duty to monitor these irregularities, but I never heard anything like that. I never witnessed anything like that. I heard no rumours at all to that effect. I received no information indicating that anything had been embezzled or that any funds were mis-administrated by the Ministry of the Interior, nothing at least within the remit of the Materials and Finances Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Bruno Stojic, having left his position as assistant minister of the interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in a formal or an informal way, was accused of any irregularities committed during his term of office?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Once Bruno Stojic had stopped travelling to Sarajevo in early April 1991, I would be physically present, I would be at the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo every day, even on Sundays, until the day I left Sarajevo with my family, which was in late June, which was a total of three months. I never came across any instance of anyone at all launching an investigation into Mr. Bruno Stojic's work or, indeed, questioning its regularity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Our last document is 2D0842. This is a letter from the Ministry of the Interior, the Sarajevo-based ministry. The date is the 17th of September, 1992. If we look at this letter, at the beginning it says that the government ordered the Ministry of the Interior to look into issues that have to do with the criminal responsibility of Branko Kvesic, Momcilo Mandic and Bruno Stojic, if any, and then the letter goes on to state what exactly the MUP had found. Without speculating, can you tell us this: Why the three names? Why do you think these three names are there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Each of these persons held a position of responsibility and authority. Each, at least the way I see it, could have been or indeed was in a position to handle public resources or perhaps resources belonging to the Ministry of the Interior, and that was a considerable amount. Each or any of these persons could potentially have found themselves in a situation where they could embezzle or misuse such funds as were available. That is why, I think, the government wanted them to look into these three persons. This was probably favoured by the fact that none of these three persons were in Sarajevo at the time. They had long stopped coming to work.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could there please be a pause between questions and answers. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Finally, the last paragraph of this document, document number 3, reads: "At the Ministry of the Interior, at this time we do not have any specific information as to irregularities committed by Bruno Stojic, the former assistant minister of the interior. Nevertheless, a revision is underway of certain segments involving material and financial transactions within the administration headed at the time by Bruno Stojic. A special report will be drawn up on this matter." Mr. Korac, do you know whether any steps were taken following this letter, any measures taken against Bruno Stojic? Were any irregularities or anything illegal at all found in his work as the assistant minister of the interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the date this document bears, and I was no longer at the ministry myself. I did go back to Sarajevo eventually in 1996. Ever since my return, and I have been socialising with people from this professional environment, I have been spending time with journalists as well, and they have spent an enormous amount of effort looking into cases such as this one, I never, ever heard anything at all about any investigations into possible irregularities that occurred in Sarajevo, and Bruno Stojic's name was never associated with any of these, not during his time with the Ministry of the Interior. There was never anything like that, not as far as I know. To the best of my knowledge, no one ever brought up his name associated to anything like that. No irregularities were ever found, nothing to do with Mr. Bruno Stojic's work during his time with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Korac. This concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D3, please, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We don't have any question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, we have no questions either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PLAVEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. We have no questions, but we do wish to thank the gentleman for coming here to give his evidence. Thank you very much, sir, and safe travels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me ask the Prosecution, will there be a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon to Your Honours. And good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. President, yes, there will be some questions. We appreciate that this not a central issue, but there will be some cross-examination, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's break for 20 minutes. Afterwards, the Prosecution will have the floor, and if need be, Ms. Nozica will have time for redirect. Then we'll have a second break, and we will resume ex parte with Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Mr. Korac, before today did you know that Mate Boban had praised Bruno Stojic for obtaining over 150 Golfs and weapons for Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I was informed about that claim regarding the vehicles during my proofing sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. And you heard Ms. Nozica refer to that conversation in the course of this afternoon's testimony, I think.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I get with you, please, two things clear. The first thing I want to get clear is the date of that conversation, and the second, just what is said. And to do that, you'll find in front of you a very small bundle of documents. The first of those is P00134. And this, we're going to see, is the source of the conversation to which you and I have just referred. All right? The first page is simply there to tell us who was present; it's Mr. Tudjman, and, at the foot of the page, Mr. Boban. And the date is the 10th of March, 1992. All right, can you see that? Now, that's at the time when Mr. Stojic --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- is still working at the MUP, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if you would turn on with me, please, we have the next page, page 103, is simply there to show us that it's Mate Boban who is speaking. And over the page, page 104, we have Mr. Boban referring to appointments and talking about appointments that have been made for the lottery and other institutions. All right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If you turn the page again with me, you'll find that we have a paragraph which, in the English, starts: "Luckily, we had a man for financial affairs in the Ministry of the Interior." Can you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And it reads: "Luckily, we had a man for financial affairs in the Ministry of the Interior, Bruno Stojic, a devoted man, whom they wanted to dismiss in writing because of this, and this man has given us so far, in our territory of Herceg-Bosna, over 150 new Golf cars, not to mention the weapons, but I can say it because this is the party." All right. And that's the conversation that you have been referred to both in your proofing session and today. Now, in March, as you've just said, Bruno Stojic is still working at the MUP; yes?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you can produce invoices which show where the cars were purchased from?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And those invoices show that the cars came from a motor car dealership in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And they relate to the MUP spending well over 80 million dinars at a time when money was very tight within the MUP, do they not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't comment. I don't know whether the money situation was tight or not. It was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, forgive me, Mr. Korac, but you've been asked to produce a document that shows Mr. Stojic trying to generate additional funds by renting out a police social club, and it perhaps is a fair observation to make that it's going to take quite a lot of rentals on a club of that kind to buy 270 Golfs. So for me to say to you that money is tight and this is 80 million dinars is a fair observation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: You will remember that I said that the funds that could be obtained in rentals were insignificant in comparison with the expenditures on the part of the ministry, and of course you could not purchase 200 and I don't know how many vehicles. But whether the financial situation was in line with the overall situation in society, I can agree that the extraordinary circumstances in the state implied that there was also an extraordinary financial situation in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're not going to waste too much time on that. That's where they came from, but as to where they were actually going, Mr. Kovac, are you saying that the best record we have is the handwritten annotations on the top of some of these pieces of paper; is that your understanding, that that's the best record of where the vehicles were going to go?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Of course not. The destination of anything, and especially something that was valuable, such as any car was, had an accompanying form. Every annotation of a vehicle was accompanied by the record of the hand-over of such a vehicle which was part of the accountancy record. The accountant in the department prepared all the necessary documents, which means that anything that was purchased and paid and became the ownership of the Ministry of the Interior in this case meant that the thing was indeed procured and that it was distributed pursuant to a regular legal procedure. I can claim that because I was a participant in the procedure, I can testify to that, and I believe that the documents in question can still be found in the files of the Ministry of the Interior, documenting each and every piece of goods purchased.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we would expend there to be a very substantial document trail in relation to the movement of these vehicles, wouldn't we? We're agreeing about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Of course there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, the reason that I ask is this: Part of the purpose of you being called to give evidence today, as we understand it, is to tell us where these vehicles went, and that's why I've asked you whether the best record available is the handwritten entry on the top of some of these pages, and it's by no means all. There are dozens of these pages that are blank, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So your evidence is that there are proper records, but you haven't got them with you and they're not in the binder that you've been asked to look at; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: The crown of every financial transaction is the accounting record of a business event. One such event is the purchase and distribution of a resource, and at the end of the year there is the legally-prescribed stock-taking of all the resources that had been purchased prior to the stock-taking exercise and that should be in the ministry. If something is not in the ministry and there is a record of its purchase, or if there was mismanagement and if the thing went missing, then this is easily established by the stock-taking exercise. Since we have established prior to this that on the 31st of December, 1991, there were no discrepancies, and I stayed with the ministry until June of the following year, and in the report produced by the government as the owner of all the resources, including the Golfs, the government requested from the Ministry of the Interior to account for the money that was supposed to be spent for the vehicles, and as a result of that there was no inquiring into anything that may have been illegal, based on which I can conclude -- not just me but everybody else can conclude that the funds had not been mis-appropriated. Every vehicle has a license. You don't have to have a take-over record, because it's a well-known fact that the ownership is well known, and it is also well known who is supposed to be looking after every vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Forgive me, sir. That was, if you don't mind me saying, a lengthy answer to what was meant to be a reasonably straightforward question. There are proper records of these transactions and where the vehicles went to, but you don't have them with you and they're not in the binder that you've been asked to look at; is that the position? I think you can answer that question simply "yes" or "no," can you not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes, it's not in the binder, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Lastly, you've told us a little bit about when Mr. Stojic left Sarajevo. We know that the last order for these cars is dated the 10th of March of 1992. The biggest of the orders is dated the 31st of December of 1991, but the last order whilst he would have been in Sarajevo is the 10th of March; yeah? And you've told us that he was in the habit of going to visit his family in Neum over the weekend and was not able to get back into Sarajevo because of the blockade which occurred at the beginning of April of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you just turn over, in the small bundle of documents that you have there, to the document that is labelled P00163. This is a document that's dated the 16th of April of 1992, and it appoints a number of people to the Command of the Grude Forward Command Post of the Southern Front, and it's over the name of General Bobetko. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: At number 7, one of the names is that of your former boss, Bruno Stojic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You told us, towards the beginning of your evidence, that Mr. Stojic, in the period at the beginning of April, was making telephone calls to the MUP, saying that he was unable to return to work because of the blockade, although, as you said, I think, you already knew that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did he mention any other engagements that he might have had in Grude at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to clarify two issues with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Korac, you had an occasion to see the documents that the federal ministry of the interior in Sarajevo submitted to Mr. Bruno Stojic's Defence regarding the Golf vehicles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you see, among the documents, that only these invoices were submitted; no other documents accompanying the hand-over of the vehicles was submitted to us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: I saw a list of documents that are listed as having been found in the offices denoted by numbers and in the cupboards in the corridors, also denoted by numbers. Among the lists, there are the hand-over records for the vehicles and so on and so forth, which are not part of my binders. In other words, the gentleman who submitted the documents also mentioned that those were found in the cupboards.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But the documents were not delivered to us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: They're not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now I would kindly ask you to tell me this: When it comes to the destination of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. Witness, how can you affirm that something has not been delivered to Ms. Nozica and the Defence of Mr. Stojic, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the record of the contents of the documents contained in a binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And at which binder would that be, please? Can you be more precise? Are you talking about the binder you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, I can refer you to a document that the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The witness should really --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I appreciate your wish to assist, but I think if I were a party, I would perhaps object, that counsel should not testify. Witness, the binder you were talking about, is it the one that we all have seen here or were you talking about another binder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I obviously refer to the list of invoices. I thought that that would be it. However, this is a list of invoices as part of the documents located in office number 24, and the document number is 2D843.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That is enough, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. This is as much as I wanted to say as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were involved in the annual stock-taking in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: After the stock-taking, did you establish or were you in a position to establish the situation of every segment of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Were you able to establish where each resource was, including the Golf vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Of course. The resources, such as vehicles, bear the chassis numbers, and that's how they are recorded in the stock-taking list. Every organisational unit involved in the stock-taking, and this refers to every public security station --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness should slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they are involved in stock-taking, they have to identify every vehicle by the chassis number. And only one such vehicle can exist in the entire world, and if it -- there's no discrepancy between the books and the actual situation, that means that the vehicle is still where it is supposed to be and where it is supposed to be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a very professional explanation. I would kindly ask you to tell us very concretely. Can you answer my question? Does this mean that every such vehicle was delivered to the public security station to which it was supposed to be delivered according to the programme, or to the police station or the security services centre which is mentioned in the invoice as the place of where that vehicle had to be delivered?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you how much money was spent to purchase the vehicles. I will ask again, although I thought it was clear. The funds in question that the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina spent in 1991 had been approved in the budget that was approved by the Government and the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KORAC
utterances.text: Of course. If that had not been the case, then there would not have been any funds.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
